common_name: Don's Variegated Florida Azalea (Gold-Edged Foliage Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil at a woodland edge with morning sun and afternoon shade; this is one of very few variegated selections of any native deciduous azalea, so protect the cream-edged foliage from harsh midday sun.

directions: Don's Variegated is a rare gold-margined sport of the Florida azalea, discovered among seedlings by Georgia plantsman Don Jacobs of Eco-Gardens in Decatur and prized as one of the very few variegated forms of any native deciduous azalea in cultivation. In late March and early April it opens fragrant, bright orange-gold trumpets with flared, curled-back petals and long exserted stamens, typically appearing just before or as the new leaves unfurl. The cream-margined foliage keeps its brightness through the growing season, giving the shrub ornamental interest well past bloom, before coloring and dropping in fall. Site in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil at a woodland edge with morning sun and afternoon shade, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the previous season's wood.

common_name: Clyo Red Piedmont Azalea (Deep Red-Pink Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in filtered or dappled shade; Clyo Red is one of the darkest-flowered Piedmont azalea selections available and can scorch in hot, exposed Southern sun.

directions: Clyo Red is the deepest-colored pink selection of Piedmont azalea yet found, discovered growing wild in Effingham County, Georgia, and introduced by Woodlanders Nursery for its saturated red-pink, tubular flowers held in showy spring clusters. Some observers note the unusually vivid color hints at natural introgression from the nearby Oconee azalea, a cross that occurs often enough in the wild to have earned its own hybrid name, though the plant is grown and sold under the Piedmont azalea epithet. It keeps the open, airy, multi-stemmed habit typical of the species rather than the dense form of evergreen garden azaleas, and its long, showy stamens draw early-spring pollinators. Give it filtered or dappled shade rather than full sun, since the foliage can scorch in hot, exposed Southern sites.

common_name: Camilla's Blush Piedmont Azalea (Blush-Pink Suckering Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained acidic soil in dappled or high open shade; Camilla's Blush spreads by suckers into a broad colony over time, so allow generous room.

directions: Camilla's Blush was selected and introduced by Jeff and Lisa Beasley of Transplant Nursery in Lavonia, Georgia, who named it for their eldest daughter, and it is valued for opening deep pink buds into soft, blush-pink-and-white fragrant flowers held in large spring clusters. Unlike many named azalea selections it spreads by suckers, gradually forming a broad multi-stemmed colony rather than staying a single specimen, which suits it well for naturalizing along a stream bank or shaded slope. Grow it in humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained acidic soil in dappled or high open shade; morning sun with afternoon shade is tolerated, but hot, exposed afternoon sites are not. Established colonies need only routine watering during dry spells once settled in.

common_name: Chocolate Drop Piedmont Azalea (Chocolate-Red New-Foliage Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; filtered light helps Chocolate Drop's red new growth hold its color without scorching.

directions: Chocolate Drop was found as a chance seedling by Ernest Koone III at Lazy K Nursery in Pine Mountain, Georgia, and is grown chiefly for its unusual foliage rather than flower color: new leaves emerge a rich chocolate-red before gradually greening, with later flushes of summer growth repeating the red color. Its white, fragrant flowers were an unexpected surprise to its discoverer, who anticipated the typical pink of straight-species Piedmont azalea, and they add a secondary season of interest against the maturing dark green leaves. The shrub keeps the same open, multi-stemmed habit and Gulf South heat tolerance as the species it was selected from. Site in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where filtered light helps the red new growth hold its color without scorching.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society

common_name: Frosty Alabama Azalea (Blue-Gray Foliage Fragrant White Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, acidic, well-drained woodland soil enriched with pine bark or leaf mold, in part shade or morning sun with afternoon protection; Frosty gently suckers into a colony over time, so allow room for gradual spread.

directions: Frosty was selected years ago in southwest Georgia by plantsman Terry Greer for its distinctive cool, blue-gray glaucous foliage, a marked departure from the plain green leaves of typical Alabama azalea seedlings. In mid to late spring it opens intensely lemon-scented white flowers with a prominent yellow blotch, held in clusters of six to ten with long, arching stamens, in what is considered among the most powerfully fragrant of the Southeast's wild deciduous azaleas. The shrub grows into a low, rounded form and gently suckers into a colony over time, so allow room for gradual spread rather than confining it to a tight foundation bed. Grow in moist, acidic, well-drained woodland soil enriched with pine bark or leaf mold, in part shade or morning sun with afternoon protection.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Nancy Callaway Alabama Azalea (Dense Spreading Fragrant White Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade, mulching to keep roots cool through Gulf South summers; Nancy Callaway keeps a noticeably tighter, more uniform habit than seedling-grown Alabama azalea.

directions: Nancy Callaway was selected at Callaway Gardens in Pine Mountain, Georgia, and named for a daughter-in-law of the garden's founders, chosen for a notably dense, low, spreading habit and glossy foliage rather than for unusual flower color. Its fragrant white flowers, marked with a yellow blotch on the upper lobe, open in the same mid-spring window as typical Alabama azalea but on a noticeably tighter, more uniform shrub, reaching roughly five feet tall and equally wide at maturity. This compact, spreading form suits a foreground shrub border or foundation planting better than the looser, taller habit of seedling-grown Alabama azalea. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade, mulching to keep roots cool through Gulf South summers.
sources: Van Landingham Glen — UNC Charlotte Botanical Gardens

common_name: Rosy Pink Pinxterbloom Azalea (Bright Pink Selected Form)

planting.note: Plant container specimens in fall in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich, very well-drained soil in partial to fairly deep shade; mulch with pine bark to maintain the acidic soil pH this species requires.

directions: Rosy Pink is a selected clone of pinxterbloom azalea offered by Pleasant Run Nursery for flowers that run noticeably brighter and pinker than the pale-pink-to-white range typical of wild seedlings of the species. Lightly fragrant flowers open on upright, twiggy, leafless stems in early spring before the foliage emerges, in the same loose, airy clusters characteristic of pinxterbloom azalea. It keeps the species' tolerance of partial shade to fairly deep shade and its preference for moist, humus-rich woodland soil, though sharp drainage is still important since wet, compacted sites will not be tolerated. Site at a woodland margin or shaded border edge, and mulch with pine bark to maintain the strongly acidic soil pH this species requires.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
